sections.heading: Lead
Synopsis
sections.wikitext:
The song begins with a spoken word segment involving two presumably thin, white [[valley girl]]s. In the background, a curvy woman slowly dances in silhouette. One of the two valley girls (dubbed Linda by Amylia Diaz-Dorsey)<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.usatoday.com/embed/video/28302693/|title=OMG, meet the real 'Becky' from 'Baby Got Back'|website=Usatoday.com|access-date=May 21, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.vulture.com/2013/12/sir-mix-a-lot-baby-got-back-video-oral-history.html|title='And I Cannot Lie': The Oral History of Sir Mix-a-Lot's 'Baby Got Back' Video|date=19 December 2013|access-date=18 June 2016|archive-date=26 June 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160626080837/http://www.vulture.com/2013/12/sir-mix-a-lot-baby-got-back-video-oral-history.html|url-status=live}}</ref> remarks to her friend, "Oh, my, God Becky, look at her butt! It is so big!" This section ends with Linda saying "she's just so... black!", at which point the verse begins.

The first verse begins with "I like big butts and I cannot lie" and the narrator's attraction to women with large buttocks is a major theme of the song. The second and third verses challenge mainstream norms of beauty with lyrics such as "I ain't talkin' 'bout ''[[Playboy]]''/'Cause silicone parts are made for toys" and "So ''[[Cosmopolitan (magazine)|Cosmo]]'' says you're fat/Well I ain't down with that!"

The song came from a meeting between Sir Mix-a-Lot and Amylia Dorsey, who saw little representation of full-figured women in media. The idea came from a 1980s-era Budweiser commercial<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2OwnwBwTg4c |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211212/2OwnwBwTg4c| archive-date=2021-12-12 |url-status=live|title=Spuds McKenzie|date=August 20, 2016|website=youtube.com|access-date=November 30, 2016}}{{cbignore}}</ref> featuring thin, valley girl-esque models of varying ethnicities. They decided to dedicate a song to the opposite, featuring curvy women of color. Mix and Dorsey sought to "broaden the definition of beauty."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.usatoday.com/videos/news/2015/06/01/28302693/|title=OMG, meet the real 'Becky' from 'Baby Got Back'|website=usatoday.com|access-date=November 30, 2016}}</ref>

Sir Mix-a-Lot commented in a 1992 interview: "The song doesn't just say I like large butts, you know? The song is talking about women who damn near kill themselves to try to look like these beanpole models that you see in ''[[Vogue (magazine)|Vogue]]'' magazine." He explained that most women respond positively to the song's message, especially black women: "They all say, 'About time.{{'"}}<ref>{{Cite journal |first=Brian |last=Keizer |date=September 1992 |title = Big Buts | journal = [[Spin (magazine)|Spin]] |volume = 8 |issue = 6 |pages = 87–88 }}</ref>

The dialogue of actress [[Papillon Soo Soo]] saying "Me so horny" is sampled from the 1987 film ''[[Full Metal Jacket]]'' to complete Sir Mix-a-Lot's lyric, "That butt you got makes..."

In 2014, according to TMZ, Sir Mix-a-Lot said it was [[Jennifer Lopez]]'s moves as a [[List of In Living Color cast members|Fly Girl]] on the 1990s show ''[[In Living Color]]'' that first inspired him to write "Baby Got Back".<ref>{{Cite magazine|url=https://www.billboard.com/music/rb-hip-hop/sir-mix-a-lot-baby-got-back-jennifer-lopez-6319546/|title=Sir Mix-A-Lot's 'Baby Got Back' Was About|magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]|date=13 November 2014|access-date=7 December 2021|archive-date=7 December 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211207034612/https://www.billboard.com/music/rb-hip-hop/sir-mix-a-lot-baby-got-back-jennifer-lopez-6319546/|url-status=live}}</ref>
sections.text:
The song begins with a spoken word segment involving two presumably thin, white valley girls. In the background, a curvy woman slowly dances in silhouette. One of the two valley girls (dubbed Linda by Amylia Diaz-Dorsey) remarks to her friend, "Oh, my, God Becky, look at her butt! It is so big!" This section ends with Linda saying "she's just so... black!", at which point the verse begins.

The first verse begins with "I like big butts and I cannot lie" and the narrator's attraction to women with large buttocks is a major theme of the song. The second and third verses challenge mainstream norms of beauty with lyrics such as "I ain't talkin' 'bout Playboy/'Cause silicone parts are made for toys" and "So Cosmo says you're fat/Well I ain't down with that!"

The song came from a meeting between Sir Mix-a-Lot and Amylia Dorsey, who saw little representation of full-figured women in media. The idea came from a 1980s-era Budweiser commercial featuring thin, valley girl-esque models of varying ethnicities. They decided to dedicate a song to the opposite, featuring curvy women of color. Mix and Dorsey sought to "broaden the definition of beauty."

Sir Mix-a-Lot commented in a 1992 interview: "The song doesn't just say I like large butts, you know? The song is talking about women who damn near kill themselves to try to look like these beanpole models that you see in Vogue magazine." He explained that most women respond positively to the song's message, especially black women: "They all say, 'About time.{{'"}}

The dialogue of actress Papillon Soo Soo saying "Me so horny" is sampled from the 1987 film Full Metal Jacket to complete Sir Mix-a-Lot's lyric, "That butt you got makes..."

In 2014, according to TMZ, Sir Mix-a-Lot said it was Jennifer Lopez's moves as a Fly Girl on the 1990s show In Living Color that first inspired him to write "Baby Got Back".

sections.heading: Critical reception
sections.wikitext:
[[Larry Flick]] from ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' magazine wrote, "First offering from rapper's major-label debut, ''[[Mack Daddy]]'', cheekily [[Rhapsody (music)|rhapsodizes]] about the joys of women with prominent backsides. Cute rhymes and slammin' beats add up to a potential smash at several formats."<ref>{{cite magazine|first= Larry |last= Flick |title= Single Reviews |magazine= [[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]] |date= February 29, 1992 |page= 72 |access-date= October 24, 2020 |url= https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-Billboard/90s/1992/Billboard-1992-02-29.pdf |author-link= Larry Flick}}</ref>

[[J. D. Considine]] from ''[[The Baltimore Sun]]'' commented, "In some cases, what's said can be as simple as Sir Mix-a-Lot's assertion 'I like big butts!' in the single 'Baby Got Back'. On the surface, it may seem that all he's doing is expressing an opinion, but there's more to it than Mix-a-Lot's personal preferences. At root, 'Baby Got Back' challenges the dominant standard for physical beauty in our culture, a standard that stresses long legs, slim hips, small buttocks and has no room for women with wide hips or protuberant posteriors. And the fact that 'Baby Got Back' spent five weeks at No. 1 suggests that there are millions who agree with his assessment."<ref>[[J.D. Considine|Considine, J.D.]] (1992). "Are today's rock stars just troublemakers or voices of discontent?". ''[[The Baltimore Sun]]''. – via ''[[Edmonton Journal]]''. (November 11, 1992).</ref>

James Bernard from ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]'' remarked that the song "alternates deftly between a critique of the [[Cosmopolitan (magazine)|''Cosmo'']]/''[[Playboy]]'' narrow-minded – and narrow-hipped – standard of female beauty and a bawdy appreciation of, er, generous rear ends."<ref>{{cite magazine |first= James |last= Bernard |title= Mack Daddy |magazine= [[Entertainment Weekly]] |date= March 13, 1992 |access-date= November 11, 2020 |url= https://ew.com/article/1992/03/13/mack-daddy/ |archive-date= December 1, 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20201201191621/https://ew.com/article/1992/03/13/mack-daddy/ |url-status= dead }}</ref>

In ''[[Melody Maker]]''{{'s}} review of the album, "Baby Got Back" was named "worst of all" and "a hip hop 'Fatty Bum Bum' and – Warning! Warning! – could be a novelty hit."<ref>{{cite magazine|author=Push|title=Albums|magazine=[[Melody Maker]]|date=January 25, 1992|page=28|access-date=February 21, 2023|url=https://www.flickr.com/photos/nothingelseon/52544485857/|archive-date=February 21, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230221194015/https://www.flickr.com/photos/nothingelseon/52544485857/|url-status=live}}</ref>

Mark Coleman from ''[[Rolling Stone]]'' said the song "celebrates a section of the anatomy long revered by rappers ("beggin' for a piece of that bubble" is a new twist)."<ref>{{Cite magazine|url=http://www.rollingstone.com/artists/sirmixalot/albums/album/241576/review/6212294/mack_daddy|title=Sir Mix-A-Lot: Mack Daddy|magazine=[[Rolling Stone]]|date=September 30, 2007|last=Coleman|first=Mark|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930221843/http://www.rollingstone.com/artists/sirmixalot/albums/album/241576/review/6212294/mack_daddy|archive-date=September 30, 2007|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 2020, [[Cleveland.com]] ranked "Baby Got Back" number 24 in their list of the best ''[[Billboard (magazine)|''Billboard'']] '' [[Hot 100]] No. 1 song of the 1990s. They described it as "the novelty song that never went away", adding, "You could put this on at a wedding today and women will recite the opening word for word before the rap breaks in and everyone (and I mean everyone) joins in. Sir Mix-a-Lot was never shy about playing up the song's "playful" nature, rapping on top of a giant butt in the video."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cleveland.com/entertainment/2020/10/every-no-1-song-of-the-1990s-ranked-from-worst-to-best.html|title=Every No. 1 song of the 1990s ranked from worst to best|first=Tony L.|last=Smith|work=[[Cleveland.com]]|date=October 21, 2020|access-date=February 5, 2021|archive-date=October 27, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221027192441/https://www.cleveland.com/entertainment/2020/10/every-no-1-song-of-the-1990s-ranked-from-worst-to-best.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

The song has been cited in demonstrating the limitations of the [[Bechdel test]], which requires that two named women talk to each other about something other than a man in order to be passed. It has been described as passing the test because it begins with a [[valley girl]] saying to another "Oh my god, Becky, look at her butt!".<ref name=LifehackerDouglas>[https://lifehacker.com/the-bechdel-test-and-other-media-representation-tests-1819324045 The Bechdel Test, and Other Media Representation Tests, Explained] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180418032535/https://lifehacker.com/the-bechdel-test-and-other-media-representation-tests-1819324045 |date=2018-04-18 }}, by Nick Douglas, at ''[[Lifehacker]]''; published October 10, 2017; retrieved April 17, 2018</ref><ref name=JezebelSimulator>[https://jezebel.com/this-bechdel-test-simulator-shows-how-easy-it-is-to-pre-1753250185 This Bechdel Test Simulator Shows How Easy It Is to Predict Who Makes Sexist Movies (Men)] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171017232421/https://jezebel.com/this-bechdel-test-simulator-shows-how-easy-it-is-to-pre-1753250185 |date=2017-10-17 }}, by Kara Brown, at ''[[Jezebel (website)|Jezebel]]''; published January 15, 2016; retrieved April 17, 2018</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Gomez Maureira |first1=M.A.|last2=Rombout|first2=L.E.|editor1-last=Chorianopoulos|editor1-first=Konstantinos|title=Entertainment Computing – ICEC 2015: 14th International Conference, ICEC 2015, Trondheim, Norway, September 29 – October 2, 2015, Proceedings|date=2015|publisher=Springer|isbn=9783319245898|page=546|chapter=Sonifying Gender Representation in Film |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vBWcCgAAQBAJ&q=%22the+sonification+process%22}}</ref>

sections.heading: Chart performance and awards
sections.wikitext: "Baby Got Back" reached number one on the US ''Billboard'' Hot 100 chart for five weeks in the summer of 1992, and won a [[1993 in music|1993]] [[Grammy Award for Best Rap Solo Performance]]. In the years following the song's release on the album ''[[Mack Daddy]]'', it has continued to appear in many movies, television shows, and commercials, as detailed below. It was ranked number six on [[VH1]]'s "Greatest Songs of the '90s", and number one on VH1's "Greatest One Hit Wonders of the '90s". In 2017, ''[[Rolling Stone]]'' magazine ranked it number 64 in their list of "100 Greatest Hip-Hop Songs of All Time".<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-lists/100-greatest-hip-hop-songs-of-all-time-105784/sir-mix-a-lot-baby-got-back-117017|title=100 Greatest Hip-Hop Songs of All Time|magazine=[[Rolling Stone]]|date=June 2, 2017|access-date=October 12, 2025}}</ref> In 2023, ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' ranked it number 327 in their "500 Best Pop Songs of All Time".<ref name="billboard500bestpopsongs" /> Same year, ''[[Time Out (magazine)|Time Out]]'' ranked "Baby Got Back" number 23 in their "The 100 Best Party Songs Ever Made".<ref>{{cite web|first1=Ella|last1=Doyle|first2=India|last2=Lawrence|first3=Henrietta|last3=Taylor|first4=James|last4=Manning|first5=Andy|last5=Kryza|first6=Andrzej|last6=Lukowski|first7=Nick|last7=Levine|first8=Chris|last8=Waywell|url=https://www.timeout.com/music/best-party-songs|title=The 100 Best Party Songs Ever Made|work=[[Time Out (magazine)|Time Out]]|date=July 28, 2023|access-date=August 8, 2024|archive-date=June 16, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220616212144/https://www.timeout.com/music/best-party-songs|url-status=live}}</ref>

sections.heading: ''Glee'' cover
sections.wikitext:

Coulton's arrangement of the song was used in a 2013 [[Sadie Hawkins (Glee)|episode]] of the musical television series ''[[Glee (TV series)|Glee]]'' without Coulton's knowledge or permission.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.avclub.com/jonathan-coulton-says-glee-ripped-off-his-cover-of-bab-1798235755 | title = Jonathan Coulton says Glee ripped off his cover of "Baby Got Back" | publisher = [[The A.V. Club]] | date = 2013-01-18 | access-date = 2013-01-27 | first = Marah | last = Eakin | archive-date = 2021-09-25 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210925001645/https://www.avclub.com/jonathan-coulton-says-glee-ripped-off-his-cover-of-bab-1798235755 | url-status = live }}</ref> Coulton publicly lambasted the show's producers, and alleged that they had even lifted elements from his recording,<ref name="cnn joco">{{cite web | url =  http://www.cnn.com/2013/01/26/showbiz/glee-coulton-song-copyright/index.html | title = Singer alleges 'Glee' ripped off his cover song | first = Elizabeth | last = Landau | date = 2013-01-26 | access-date = 2013-01-27 | publisher = [[CNN]] }}</ref> but claimed that Fox responded that "they're within their legal rights to do this, and that [Coulton] should be happy for the exposure", though Coulton pointed out that he was not credited within the episode.<ref name="cnn joco"/> Coulton released his cover of "Baby Got Back" to iTunes, labelling it "a cover of Glee's cover of my cover of Sir Mix-a-Lot's song", with proceeds going to charity.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.forbes.com/sites/michelecatalano/2013/01/27/jonathan-coulton-vs-glee-its-about-the-ethics/ | title = Jonathan Coulton vs. Glee: It's About the Ethics | first = Michele | last = Cantalano | date = 2013-01-27 | access-date = 2013-01-27 | work = [[Forbes]] | archive-date = 2013-01-29 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20130129183134/http://www.forbes.com/sites/michelecatalano/2013/01/27/jonathan-coulton-vs-glee-its-about-the-ethics/ | url-status = live }}</ref> Coulton pursued legal charges against the show's producers, but ultimately dropped them, deciding a seeming victory in the court of public opinion was "a good enough win." The controversy was referenced in a season 5 episode of ''[[The Good Wife]]'' entitled [[The Good Wife season 5|"Goliath and David"]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Lorre |first1=Rose Maura |title=Jonathan Coulton on Seeing His Glee Flap Play out on The Good Wife |url=https://www.vulture.com/2014/01/jonathan-coulton-interview-good-wife-glee.html |website=Vulture |date=7 January 2014 |publisher=New York |access-date=17 July 2023 |archive-date=17 July 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230717124327/https://www.vulture.com/2014/01/jonathan-coulton-interview-good-wife-glee.html |url-status=live }}</ref>
sections.text:
Jonathan Coulton released a cover of "Baby Got Back" during his Thing a Week project in October 2005, with the song being released as part of the first Thing A Week compilation album the next year. Coulton performs the song on acoustic guitar with a gentle and tender melody at odds with the lascivious nature of the lyrics.

Coulton's arrangement of the song was used in a 2013 episode of the musical television series Glee without Coulton's knowledge or permission. Coulton publicly lambasted the show's producers, and alleged that they had even lifted elements from his recording, but claimed that Fox responded that "they're within their legal rights to do this, and that [Coulton] should be happy for the exposure", though Coulton pointed out that he was not credited within the episode. Coulton released his cover of "Baby Got Back" to iTunes, labelling it "a cover of Glee's cover of my cover of Sir Mix-a-Lot's song", with proceeds going to charity. Coulton pursued legal charges against the show's producers, but ultimately dropped them, deciding a seeming victory in the court of public opinion was "a good enough win." The controversy was referenced in a season 5 episode of The Good Wife entitled "Goliath and David".

sections.heading: Related songs
sections.wikitext:

Black men like butts. In a 2000 interview, Sir Mix-a-Lot reflected, "There's always butt songs. Hell, I got the idea sitting up here listening to old Parliament records: Motor Booty Affair. Black men like butts. That's the bottom line." The song is part of a tradition of 1970s–90s African-American music celebrating the female posterior, including "Da Butt", "Rump Shaker", and "Shake Your Groove Thing".

In 2014, Trinidadian-American rapper Nicki Minaj sampled "Baby Got Back", including some of its verses, for her hit "Anaconda", from the album The Pinkprint. The song has been viewed by some as a diss track, in answer to "Baby Got Back". Whereas Sir Mix-a-Lot "sings the praises of the Black female body, but his focus remains on the pleasure it provides for the appreciative Black man", Minaj raps from the perspective of the unnamed woman, "giving voice to the woman who profits from her callipygian physique".

In the Horrible Histories television series, a parody song uses the rhythm and call-and-response structure of "Baby Got Back" to retell the failures of over-ambitious royal flagships: The White Ship (1120), The Mary Rose (1545) and The Vasa (1628).
